newsitem.title: RUSSIA: Yeltsin boasts of good health, backs new reforms.
newsitem.headline: Yeltsin boasts of good health, backs new reforms.

text.p: President Boris Yeltsin, keeping up a hectic workload during his summer vacation, boasted on Wednesday of his robust health and approved a fresh flurry of reforms aimed at reviving Russia's sluggish economy.

Yeltsin, 66, who has staged a remarkable recovery this year from heart surgery and pneumonia, held talks with First Deputy Prime Minister Boris Nemtsov and other leaders at the Volzhsky Utyos resort by the river Volga in central Russia.
He signed decrees aimed at relieving chronic delays in payment of state salaries, clamping down on tax debtors and increasing gold exports.
Nemtsov, a liberal who is also energy minister, has paid regular visits to Yeltsin during the president's vacation to win his backing for documents needed to continue reforms.

He was accompanied on Wednesday by Central Bank chairman Sergei Dubinin, who discussed gold export policy with Yeltsin and told Interfax news agency that Russia would sell only gold which it mined and not gold from its reserves.

Though on holiday since early July, Yeltsin has made quite clear that he remains in charge, firing off a steady salvo of commands on a wide range of issues from army reform to tax dodgers while enjoying his hobbies of fishing and tennis.
One of the visitors to Volzhsky Utyos in recent days has been Renat Akchurin, who performed the quintuple bypass on Yeltsin's heart last November.
Yeltsin said he discovered he could stand the heat of a Russian banya (sauna) better than the cardiac surgeon.
"In order to prove to him that my heart works like a clock, I took him to the banya," NTV commercial television showed him telling reporters.
"First he worked on me with the birch twigs and then I worked on him. We found out that his pulse was quicker than mine after that."
A bundle of birch twigs is traditionally used in the Russian banya to invigorate the blood circulation.

Yeltsin delighted human rights groups and outraged his communist and nationalist opponents on Tuesday by vetoing a controversial bill that would have imposed tough curbs on evangelical Christians, Roman Catholics and other "non-traditional" religious groups.

In a statement released by the Kremlin on Wednesday, he defended his veto of the draft law, "On Freedom of Conscience and Religious Association," saying it contradicted Russia's constitution guaranteeing equality for all confessions.

"Of course the state can and must limit the activity of pseudo-religious organisations that bring harm to the morality and health of the population. But this does not mean the state can trample on fundamental human rights," the statement said.

His veto of a bill overwhelmingly approved by both houses of parliament and strongly endorsed by the powerful Russian Orthodox Church showed Yeltsin had not lost his taste for taking risks and cocking a snook at his political opponents.

Prominent communist Viktor Iluykhin, referring to a threat by U.S. senators to withhold around $200 million worth of aid if the bill became law, said Yeltsin's veto showed yet again that Russia had become a protectorate of the West.
Archbishop Sergiy of the Orthodox Church's Holy Synod told Itar-Tass news agency that all Orthodox believers would be disappointed.
"From our point of view the law...objectively reflected the religious situation in the country. (The veto) evokes great regret and surprise among Orthodox people," he said.
